finding.claim: /transfer never validates that amount is positive. A negative amount passes the balance check and reverses the transfer, so the caller takes money from any other account. Self-transfer is also unrestricted. /withdraw does check amount <= 0, so this check is missing only here.
finding.source: Authenticated user's JSON body field `amount` (e.g. -1000) and `to` (victim account)

trace.note: to = request.json['to'] taken from the request without validation
amount = request.json['amount'] taken from the request with no type or sign validation
BAL[g.user] < amount is false for negative amount, so the check passes
BAL[to] += (-X) debits the victim with no consent

finding.guards_checked: Only the balance check at line 11 exists. There is no amount > 0 check, unlike withdraw at line 21. There is no check on the recipient and no authorization from the victim. No type validation: float, NaN, or bool values are accepted.

verdict.guard_found: Only the balance check `BAL[g.user] < amount` at bank.py:11. It is false for negative amounts, so it doesn't block them. There is no amount > 0 check, no type check, and no recipient or consent check. No before_request hook or decorator exists in the file. g.user is never set in this file, so authentication is presumably handled elsewhere. Even so, any authenticated user can reach the route.
verdict.reason: bank.py:11 only tests `BAL[g.user] < amount`, which passes for a negative amount, so lines 13-14 credit the caller and debit `to`. The `amount <= 0` guard exists only in /withdraw at bank.py:21.

verdict_facts.guard_found: Only the balance check at bank.py:11 (BAL[g.user] < amount, abort(400)); no amount > 0 check, no type validation, no recipient restriction. No decorators or other middleware in this directory.
verdict_facts.reason: bank.py:11 only checks BAL[g.user] < amount, which a negative amount always fails to trigger, so bank.py:13-14 credit the caller and debit the victim, while /withdraw at bank.py:21 has the missing amount <= 0 check; any authenticated user can reach it.

finding.claim: Check-then-act race on balances with no lock or atomic update. Concurrent requests can each pass the balance check before any deduction, so the attacker overdraws or double-spends. The same pattern exists in /withdraw at line 21.
finding.source: Multiple simultaneous POST /transfer or /withdraw requests from the same user
finding.sink: BAL[g.user] -= amount (bank.py:13, 23) on a shared global dict

trace.note: Deduction happens later, non-atomically, so other threads can interleave
Same TOCTOU in withdraw, with the check at line 21 and the deduction at line 23

finding.guards_checked: No lock, transaction, or atomic operation. BAL is an in-process global dict, so multi-threaded or multi-worker deployments are affected. The window is narrow under the CPython GIL but real.

verdict.reason: bank.py:11 checks BAL[g.user] < amount and bank.py:13 deducts it, and withdraw does the same at bank.py:21 and 23, with no lock or atomic update. Concurrent requests from one authenticated user in a threaded worker can interleave, but the window is only a few bytecodes under the GIL. Separate worker processes each have their own BAL, which is a different problem.

verdict_facts.reason: bank.py:11-13 and 21-23 check BAL[g.user] and then subtract it in separate bytecode steps with no lock or atomic update. Any authenticated user can send concurrent requests to a threaded or multi-worker server and overdraw. The window is narrow under the GIL, and with multiple workers each process has its own BAL, which is a separate consistency problem.

finding.claim: No authentication is set up. g.user is read but nothing in the app (no before_request or auth decorator) sets it. If an upstream layer populates it from a client-controlled value, there is no verification here. The endpoints also don't check that `to` exists or that the user has an account, and lookups use unguarded dict indexing.
finding.source: Any unauthenticated client; depends on how g.user is populated outside this file
finding.sink: BAL[g.user] and BAL[to] on the balance store (bank.py:11-14, 21-23)

trace.note: g.user used as identity without being set or verified in this file

finding.guards_checked: Searched the only source file. There is no before_request, login_required, or session handling. Impact depends on out-of-tree middleware. In this file alone, requests would raise AttributeError (500) rather than succeed, so this is a conditional finding.

verdict.reason: bank.py:11 and :21 read g.user and bank.py:7/:18 have no auth decorator, but nothing in this file (the only source file) ever sets g.user, so every request raises AttributeError (500); whether it is exploitable depends on out-of-tree code that populates g.user, which I can't see.

verdict_facts.guard_found: Identity (g.user) is set by trusted upstream middleware per the project facts. Nothing in bank.py itself sets or checks it.
verdict_facts.reason: The trace lines are accurate (bank.py:7, 11, 18), but the "no authentication" claim fails because g.user is set by trusted upstream middleware, and the unguarded BAL[g.user] and BAL[to] lookups at bank.py:11-14 and 21-23 only raise KeyError (a 500), which is robustness rather than a security flaw. Separately, /transfer has no `amount <= 0` check (bank.py:11-14) unlike /withdraw (bank.py:21), so a negative amount lets a user pull funds from another account. That is a different finding from F3.
